summary: This chapter covers how a registered nurse decides who to see first, which tasks can be handed to other team members, and how to protect each client's rights. These ideas are tested often, because a safe nurse must think about priorities and responsibility before acting.

When several clients need you, airway comes first, then breathing, then circulation. An unstable or newly changed client comes before a stable one, and an acute problem comes before a chronic one. When you delegate, you hand a stable, routine task with a predictable result to a licensed practical nurse or an assistive person, but you stay accountable. Assessment, teaching, care planning and judging results stay with the RN.

Clients have the right to make their own choices, including the right to refuse care. Before a procedure, the provider explains it and gets informed consent, and the nurse may witness the signature. Health information is shared only with people directly involved in care. An advance directive tells the team the client's wishes in advance, and a structured handoff such as SBAR keeps care continuous between shifts.

concepts.definition: A way to decide who needs care first. Airway problems come first, then breathing, then circulation. An unstable client, or one whose condition has suddenly changed, comes before a stable client with an expected problem. An acute, new problem comes before a chronic, expected one.
concepts.tip: Ask yourself: which client could die or be harmed first if I wait? Go to that client.

concepts.definition: Handing a task to another team member, such as a licensed practical nurse or an assistive person, while the RN stays responsible for the outcome. Only stable, routine tasks with predictable results should be delegated.
concepts.tip: The RN keeps assessment, teaching, care planning and evaluation. Bathing, feeding and routine vital signs on stable clients can be delegated.

concepts.definition: Right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, and right supervision and evaluation. All five must be in place before a task is handed off.
concepts.tip: If any one 'right' is missing, such as an unstable client or an untrained helper, do not delegate.

concepts.definition: The client's agreement to a procedure after learning its purpose, risks, benefits and other options. The provider must explain it. The nurse may witness the signature and confirms the client understands and is not sedated or confused.
concepts.tip: If the client still has questions, stop and call the provider. Do not explain the procedure risks yourself.

concepts.definition: Keeping client health information private. Share it only with people directly caring for the client or those the client has approved. Do not discuss clients in hallways, elevators or on social media.
concepts.tip: Ask: does this person need this information to care for the client? If not, do not share it.

concepts.definition: A legal document that states a client's wishes for future care. A living will lists treatments the client wants or refuses. A health care power of attorney names a person to make decisions if the client cannot.
concepts.tip: Living will = 'what' the client wants. Power of attorney = 'who' decides.

concepts.definition: A structured way to report: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. It is used for shift reports and for calling a provider about a change in the client.
concepts.tip: Have the latest vital signs, recent labs and your concern ready before you call.

points: Choose the client with an airway, breathing or circulation problem, or a sudden change, as the first to see.
Assessment, teaching, care planning and evaluation cannot be delegated to an assistive person.
The provider obtains informed consent; the nurse witnesses it and calls the provider if the client has questions.
A competent adult may refuse any treatment, even if the team disagrees.
An incident report is a quality tool; do not mention it in the client's chart.
Use SBAR when calling a provider about a change in condition.

summary: This chapter is about keeping clients and staff safe. You will learn how germs spread and which precautions stop them, how to identify clients correctly, and how to prevent falls and use restraints safely. Emergency steps, such as what to do in a fire, also belong here.

Standard precautions apply to every client, every time: clean your hands and use gloves and other protection when you may touch body fluids. Transmission-based precautions are added for certain germs. Airborne precautions need a fitted respirator and a special room, droplet precautions need a mask when close to the client, and contact precautions need a gown and gloves.

Before any medicine, test or treatment, check two client identifiers, such as name and date of birth, and never use the room number. Restraints are a last resort, need a provider order, and must be checked often. For a fire, remember RACE for the steps and PASS for using an extinguisher.

concepts.definition: Basic infection control used with every client. Clean your hands before and after care, and wear gloves, a gown, a mask or eye protection when you may touch blood or body fluids.
concepts.tip: Treat all body fluids as if they could spread infection, no matter the diagnosis.

concepts.definition: Used for germs that float in the air for a long time, such as tuberculosis, measles and chickenpox. The client stays in a negative-pressure room with the door closed, and staff wear a fitted N95 respirator.
concepts.tip: 'My Chicken Hez TB': Measles, Chickenpox (varicella), Herpes zoster spread through the body, TB.

concepts.definition: Used for germs spread by large droplets from coughing or sneezing, such as influenza, pertussis (whooping cough) and some types of meningitis. Staff wear a surgical mask when close to the client.
concepts.tip: Droplets fall quickly, so a regular mask is enough. A private room is preferred.

concepts.definition: Used for germs spread by touch, such as MRSA and C. difficile. Staff wear a gown and gloves, and equipment such as a stethoscope stays in the room.
concepts.tip: For C. difficile, wash hands with soap and water. Alcohol hand rub does not kill its spores.

concepts.definition: Before giving medicine or care, confirm the client with two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth. The room or bed number is never an identifier.
concepts.tip: Ask the client to state their name and birth date; do not just ask 'Are you Mr. Lee?'

concepts.definition: Restraints are used only when other ways have failed and the client may harm self or others. They need a provider order, must be tied to the bed frame with a quick-release knot, and the client is checked often for skin, circulation and needs.
concepts.tip: Never tie restraints to the side rail. Try less restrictive options first, such as a sitter or moving the client near the station.

concepts.definition: RACE is the order of actions in a fire: Rescue clients in danger, Alarm, Contain the fire by closing doors, Extinguish or Evacuate. PASS is how to use an extinguisher: Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side.
concepts.tip: Rescue comes first. Aim at the base of the fire, not the flames.

points: Match each disease to the right precaution: TB and measles airborne, influenza droplet, MRSA and C. difficile contact.
Use soap and water, not alcohol rub, for C. difficile.
A room number is never a client identifier.
Tie restraints to the bed frame, not the side rail, and try less restrictive options first.
In a fire, rescue clients in immediate danger before anything else.
Never recap a used needle; put it straight into a sharps container.

summary: This chapter follows a person from before birth through old age. It covers normal growth and development, care during pregnancy, labor and the weeks after birth, and care of the newborn. Knowing what is normal helps you spot what is not.

During pregnancy, teach the client to report danger signs right away, such as vaginal bleeding, a severe headache, vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, fluid leaking, or the baby moving less. High blood pressure with these signs may point to preeclampsia. During labor, watch the fetal heart rate pattern; a late deceleration suggests the baby is not getting enough oxygen through the placenta.

After birth, check the fundus often. It should be firm and in the middle; a soft fundus needs massage, and a fundus pushed to one side often means a full bladder. Lochia changes from red to pinkish-brown to whitish over the following weeks. For children, know the main milestones and Erikson's stages, so you can match care and teaching to the child's age.

concepts.definition: Signs that need quick reporting: vaginal bleeding, severe headache, blurred vision or spots, sudden swelling of the face or hands, leaking fluid, fever, or less fetal movement.
concepts.tip: Headache plus vision changes plus swelling: think preeclampsia and check the blood pressure.

concepts.definition: A pregnancy condition with new high blood pressure, usually after 20 weeks, with signs of organ stress such as protein in the urine, headache or vision changes. It can lead to seizures (eclampsia).
concepts.tip: Magnesium sulfate is used to prevent seizures; watch reflexes, breathing and urine output, and keep calcium gluconate nearby.

source.org: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

concepts.definition: A normal baseline is about 110 to 160 beats per minute. Early decelerations come from head pressure and are harmless. Late decelerations suggest poor blood flow through the placenta. Variable decelerations suggest cord compression.
concepts.tip: Remember VEAL CHOP: Variable-Cord, Early-Head, Accelerations-OK, Late-Placenta.

source.org: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

concepts.definition: Turn the client to her side, stop any oxytocin infusion, give oxygen and IV fluids as ordered, and notify the provider.
concepts.tip: Think 'more blood and oxygen to the placenta': position, stop oxytocin, fluids, oxygen.

concepts.definition: After birth the uterus should feel firm and be in the midline. A soft, boggy fundus can lead to heavy bleeding, so massage it. A fundus that is high and pushed to one side usually means a full bladder.
concepts.tip: Boggy: massage. Off to the side: help the client empty her bladder.

concepts.definition: Vaginal discharge after birth. It changes from red (rubra) to pinkish-brown (serosa) to whitish (alba). Large clots, a bad smell or a return to bright red bleeding should be reported.
concepts.tip: Red, then pink, then white: 'Rubra, Serosa, Alba'.

concepts.definition: Each age has a main task: infants learn trust, toddlers independence (autonomy), preschoolers initiative, school-age children industry, teens identity, and older adults integrity.
concepts.tip: Let toddlers make simple choices; let teens have privacy and talk to them directly.

points: Know the pregnancy danger signs that must be reported right away.
Match each fetal heart rate deceleration to its cause with VEAL CHOP.
For late decelerations: side position, stop oxytocin, fluids, oxygen, call the provider.
A boggy fundus is massaged; a fundus pushed to one side points to a full bladder.
Lochia goes from red to pink to white; heavy bleeding or a bad smell is not normal.
Match teaching to Erikson's stage, for example giving toddlers simple choices.

summary: This chapter is about keeping people healthy before illness starts or catching it early. It covers vaccines, health screening, risk factors and how to teach clients so they can care for themselves.

Prevention has three levels. Primary prevention stops a disease from starting, such as a vaccine or quitting smoking. Secondary prevention finds disease early through screening, such as a mammogram or a blood pressure check. Tertiary prevention limits harm from a disease the person already has, such as rehabilitation after a stroke.

Live vaccines, such as MMR and varicella, are generally avoided in pregnancy and in people with a badly weakened immune system. Good teaching starts by checking whether the client is ready to learn, then uses plain words, short sessions and the teach-back method.

concepts.definition: Actions that stop a disease from starting in a healthy person, such as vaccines, seat belts, a healthy diet, exercise and stopping smoking.
concepts.tip: Primary = before the disease exists.

concepts.definition: Screening and early detection to find a disease before it causes symptoms, such as blood pressure checks, mammograms and colon cancer screening.
concepts.tip: Secondary = finding it early.

concepts.definition: Care that limits damage and prevents problems from a disease the person already has, such as cardiac rehabilitation or foot care teaching for diabetes.
concepts.tip: Tertiary = living as well as possible with the disease.

concepts.definition: Vaccines made from weakened live germs, such as MMR and varicella. They are generally not given during pregnancy or to people with a severely weakened immune system.
concepts.tip: Ask about pregnancy and immune problems before giving a live vaccine.

concepts.definition: Before teaching, check that the client is comfortable, not in severe pain or anxiety, and interested. Teaching a client who is not ready rarely works.
concepts.tip: Treat pain and calm fear first, then teach.

concepts.definition: Ask the client to explain or show, in their own words, what you just taught. It checks understanding without making the client feel tested.
concepts.tip: Say 'Show me how you will check your blood sugar at home,' not 'Do you understand?'

points: Sort actions into primary, secondary or tertiary prevention; most screening is secondary prevention.
Check for pregnancy and immune problems before giving a live vaccine.
Assess readiness and remove barriers such as pain before teaching.
Use teach-back to confirm learning instead of yes-or-no questions.
Use plain language and short sessions, and include family when the client agrees.

summary: This chapter teaches how to talk with clients in a way that helps them. It also covers how people cope with illness and loss, how to help in a crisis, how to respond to abuse, and how to respect culture and language.

Therapeutic responses keep the focus on the client's feelings. Open-ended questions and reflecting feelings invite the client to talk. Responses that block talk include 'why' questions, false reassurance, giving your own advice, changing the subject and talking about yourself.

Grief often moves through denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance, but not always in order. In a crisis, focus on safety and the problem right now. Nurses must report suspected child abuse, and often elder abuse as state law requires, and a client facing partner violence should be interviewed alone. When a client speaks another language, use a trained medical interpreter, not a family member.

concepts.definition: A question that cannot be answered with yes or no, such as 'What has this week been like for you?' It invites the client to share feelings.
concepts.tip: Start with 'Tell me about...', 'How...' or 'What...'.

concepts.definition: Naming the feeling you hear and giving it back to the client, such as 'You sound frightened about the surgery.'
concepts.tip: On the exam, the right answer often names a feeling and keeps the focus on the client.

concepts.definition: Replies that shut down talk: 'why' questions, false reassurance ('Everything will be fine'), giving advice, changing the subject, or talking about yourself.
concepts.tip: Cross out any answer that promises a good outcome or asks 'why'.

concepts.definition: A common way to describe grief: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. People may skip stages or go back and forth.
concepts.tip: Bargaining often sounds like 'If I can just live until my daughter's wedding...'.

concepts.definition: Short-term help focused on the problem happening now. First make sure the client is safe, then help the client find support and next steps.
concepts.tip: Safety first, then the here and now. Deep past issues wait.

concepts.definition: Nurses must report suspected child abuse or neglect in every state. Duties to report abuse of older or dependent adults are set by state law and vary by state. Proof is not needed; reasonable suspicion is enough.
concepts.tip: Interview a client about possible abuse alone, away from the partner or caregiver.

concepts.definition: A trained interpreter is used when the client and nurse do not share a language. Family members, especially children, should not interpret health information.
concepts.tip: Speak to the client, not the interpreter, and use short sentences.

points: Pick the response that is open-ended and focused on the client's feelings.
Avoid 'why' questions, false reassurance and giving advice.
Grief stages do not always happen in order.
Suspected child abuse must be reported; elder abuse reporting rules vary by state. Suspicion is enough.
Interview a possible abuse victim alone and use a trained interpreter when needed.

compare.title: Helpful and unhelpful replies
rows: 'Tell me more about what scares you.'
'What made it hard to take them?'

summary: This chapter covers caring for clients with anxiety, mood disorders, psychosis, confusion and substance use. Safety is the main theme: protecting clients from harming themselves or others while treating them with respect.

Ask about suicide directly and clearly. A client with a plan and a way to carry it out is at high risk, and a sudden calm after deep depression can be a warning sign. Keep the area free of harmful objects. Delirium starts suddenly and often has a physical cause, while dementia develops slowly over time.

Alcohol withdrawal can begin within hours of the last drink and can become life-threatening, with tremors, sweating, fast heart rate and seizures; it is treated with benzodiazepines and thiamine. Some psychiatric drugs need close watching: lithium needs steady fluid and salt intake and blood levels, MAO inhibitors require avoiding foods high in tyramine, and clozapine can lower white blood cells.

concepts.definition: Ask directly: 'Are you thinking about killing yourself?' Then ask about a plan, the means and timing. Asking does not put the idea in the client's head.
concepts.tip: A sudden calm or giving away belongings after depression can mean the client has decided on a plan.

concepts.definition: A sudden change in attention and thinking, often over hours or days, caused by a physical problem such as infection, drugs or low oxygen. It usually improves when the cause is treated.
concepts.tip: Sudden confusion in an older adult: look for infection, drugs or low oxygen first.

concepts.definition: Symptoms such as shaking, sweating, anxiety, fast heart rate and high blood pressure can begin within hours of the last drink. Severe cases cause seizures and delirium tremens. Benzodiazepines are the main treatment.
concepts.tip: Give thiamine as ordered to prevent brain damage (Wernicke's), and keep seizure precautions.

concepts.definition: Lithium treats bipolar disorder but has a narrow safe range. Dehydration and low salt intake raise the level and can cause toxicity, with vomiting, diarrhea, coarse tremor and confusion.
concepts.tip: Teach steady fluids and steady salt, and keep regular blood level checks.

concepts.definition: MAO inhibitors are antidepressants. Eating foods high in tyramine, such as aged cheese, cured meats and draft beer, can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure.
concepts.tip: Severe headache in a client on an MAO inhibitor: think high blood pressure crisis.

concepts.definition: A rare, life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic drugs with high fever, very stiff muscles, confusion and unstable vital signs.
concepts.tip: High fever plus rigid muscles after an antipsychotic: stop the drug and call the provider right away.

concepts.definition: A safe, structured unit setting that supports healing. It includes removing harmful objects, clear rules, a calm space and consistent staff responses.
concepts.tip: Start with the least restrictive step, such as talking calmly, before seclusion or restraints.

points: Ask about suicide directly and check for a plan and means.
A sudden calm or giving things away after depression may signal suicide risk.
Delirium is sudden and often reversible; dementia is gradual.
Alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures; benzodiazepines and thiamine are key.
Teach steady fluid and salt intake for lithium and tyramine limits for MAO inhibitors.
Clozapine needs white blood cell monitoring; report fever or sore throat.

summary: This chapter covers everyday care that keeps clients comfortable and prevents problems. It includes moving and positioning, elimination, eating and drinking safely, hygiene, sleep and comfort measures that do not use medicine.

Lying still for long periods harms almost every body system. It can cause pressure injuries, blood clots, pneumonia, constipation and weak muscles. Turn and reposition clients regularly, help them walk as early as allowed, and teach coughing and deep breathing. When using a cane, hold it on the strong side and move it with the weak leg.

Aspiration happens when food or fluid goes into the lungs. Sit the client upright to eat, have clients with swallowing problems tuck the chin, and use thickened liquids if a swallowing specialist orders them. Comfort can also come from non-drug methods such as heat or cold, position changes, massage, music, guided imagery and distraction.

concepts.definition: Problems caused by staying still too long: pressure injuries, blood clots in the legs, pneumonia, constipation, muscle loss and stiff joints.
concepts.tip: Prevent them with regular turning, early walking, fluids, and coughing and deep breathing.

concepts.definition: Relieve pressure over bony areas, keep skin clean and dry, use pressure-relieving surfaces and support good nutrition. Do not massage reddened bony areas.
concepts.tip: Look at heels, hips and the tailbone area at every skin check.

concepts.definition: Steps to keep food and fluid out of the lungs: sit upright to eat, small bites, chin tuck for swallowing problems, thickened liquids as ordered, and staying upright after meals.
concepts.tip: Coughing, choking or a wet, gurgly voice while eating suggests aspiration; stop and assess.

concepts.definition: Hold the cane on the strong side. Move the cane and the weak leg together, then step through with the strong leg.
concepts.tip: On stairs: 'Up with the good, down with the bad.'

concepts.definition: Lift or roll the walker forward, step into it with the weak leg first, then bring the strong leg forward. Do not climb stairs with a standard walker.
concepts.tip: Stand inside the walker frame, not behind it.

concepts.definition: Ways to ease pain or stress without medicine: heat or cold, repositioning, massage of non-injured areas, music, guided imagery, breathing exercises and distraction.
concepts.tip: Use them together with prescribed pain medicine, not as a replacement when strong pain is present.

points: Name the complications of immobility and how to prevent each one.
Do not massage reddened skin over a bony area.
Sit the client upright to eat and use a chin tuck for swallowing problems.
Hold a cane on the strong side; on stairs, up with the good, down with the bad.
Non-drug comfort measures add to pain medicine, not replace it.

Up with good, down with bad

summary: This chapter covers giving medicines safely by any route, watching for side effects and interactions, giving blood products, caring for IV lines and managing pain. Errors here can be fatal, so the exam tests safety checks and early warning signs.

Every dose is checked against the rights of medication administration, including the right client, drug, dose, route, time and documentation. Some drugs need a check before each dose. Take an apical pulse for one full minute before digoxin. Warfarin is monitored with the INR and reversed with vitamin K, while heparin is monitored with the aPTT and reversed with protamine sulfate. When mixing insulins, draw up the clear insulin before the cloudy one.

High-alert drugs such as insulin, heparin, opioids and concentrated potassium chloride cause the most harm when given wrong; potassium chloride is never pushed IV. During a blood transfusion, stay with the client at the start, when reactions are most likely. If a reaction appears, stop the blood at once, keep the IV open with normal saline, and notify the provider and the blood bank.

concepts.definition: Checks done before every dose: right client, right drug, right dose, right route, right time and right documentation. Many lists add right reason and right response.
concepts.tip: Do the checks at the bedside with two client identifiers, not only at the medicine cart.

concepts.definition: Before giving digoxin, count the apical pulse for one full minute and hold the dose if it is below the ordered limit, often 60 in adults. Low potassium raises the risk of toxicity.
concepts.tip: Nausea, poor appetite and yellow-green vision or halos can be early signs of toxicity.

concepts.definition: Warfarin is a pill monitored with the PT/INR and reversed with vitamin K. Heparin is given by injection or IV, monitored with the aPTT, and reversed with protamine sulfate.
concepts.tip: Teach warfarin clients to keep vitamin K foods, such as leafy greens, steady rather than avoid them.

concepts.definition: When drawing regular and NPH insulin into one syringe, draw the clear regular insulin first, then the cloudy NPH. Long-acting insulins such as glargine are not mixed with others.
concepts.tip: 'Clear before cloudy.'

concepts.definition: Drugs that cause serious harm if given wrongly, including insulin, heparin, opioids and concentrated potassium chloride. Many facilities require a second nurse to double-check them.
concepts.tip: Potassium chloride is never given by IV push.

concepts.definition: Signs include fever, chills, back pain, itching, hives, low blood pressure and trouble breathing. Stop the transfusion, keep the IV open with normal saline using new tubing, and notify the provider and blood bank.
concepts.tip: Stay with the client for the first part of the transfusion, when reactions are most likely. Use only normal saline with blood.

concepts.definition: Opioids relieve pain but can slow breathing. Check sedation level and breathing before and after doses. Naloxone reverses opioid effects.
concepts.tip: Increasing sleepiness comes before slowed breathing; act early.

points: Check the apical pulse for one full minute before digoxin.
Match each blood thinner to its lab test and antidote.
Draw clear insulin before cloudy when mixing.
Never give potassium chloride by IV push.
For a transfusion reaction, stop the blood, keep the line open with normal saline and notify.
Watch sedation and breathing with opioids; naloxone reverses them.

summary: This chapter is about lowering the chance that a test, procedure or treatment harms the client. It covers vital sign changes, common lab values, preparing clients for tests, and spotting early complications after surgery and procedures.

Lab ranges differ a little between labs, so learn the commonly cited adult values and what a value far outside them means. Potassium is about 3.5 to 5.0 and sodium about 135 to 145 mEq/L. Fasting blood glucose is about 70 to 99 mg/dL. Platelets are about 150,000 to 400,000 per cubic millimeter.

Before a procedure, confirm consent, allergies such as to contrast dye, and fasting status as ordered. After a cardiac catheterization, check the insertion site for bleeding and the pulses below it, and keep the limb straight. After thyroid surgery, watch for low calcium. After any surgery, encourage the incentive spirometer and early walking. If a wound opens and organs come through, cover them with sterile saline-moistened dressings and call the surgeon.

concepts.definition: Commonly cited adult range is about 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L. Both low and high levels can cause dangerous heart rhythms.
concepts.tip: Any potassium problem: check the heart monitor.

concepts.definition: Commonly cited adult range is about 135 to 145 mEq/L. Abnormal sodium mainly affects the brain, causing confusion and, in severe cases, seizures.
concepts.tip: Sodium problems show up as changes in thinking and alertness.

concepts.definition: Fasting blood glucose is commonly cited as about 70 to 99 mg/dL. Platelets are about 150,000 to 400,000 per cubic millimeter; a low count raises bleeding risk.
concepts.tip: With low platelets, use bleeding precautions: soft toothbrush, electric razor, no IM injections if possible.

source.org: American Diabetes Association, Standards of Care

concepts.definition: Check the insertion site for bleeding or swelling, and check pulses, color and warmth below the site. Keep the affected arm or leg straight as ordered.
concepts.tip: A cool, pale limb with a weak pulse below the site needs a report right away.

concepts.definition: Watch the airway and for signs of low calcium, such as tingling around the mouth or in the fingers and muscle spasms. Damage to nearby glands can cause this.
concepts.tip: Chvostek's sign is a face twitch when the cheek is tapped; Trousseau's sign is a hand spasm with a blood pressure cuff.

concepts.definition: Organs push out through an opened surgical wound. Cover them with sterile dressings moistened with sterile saline, keep the client calm, place in low Fowler's with knees bent, and notify the surgeon.
concepts.tip: Never try to push the organs back in.

concepts.definition: A device that helps the client take slow, deep breaths after surgery to keep the lungs open and prevent atelectasis and pneumonia.
concepts.tip: Teach: breathe out, seal lips, breathe in slowly and deeply, hold, then relax.

points: Know commonly cited adult ranges for potassium, sodium, glucose and platelets, and that labs vary slightly.
Check allergies, consent and fasting status before a procedure.
After a catheterization, check the site and the pulses below it.
After thyroid surgery, watch the airway and for signs of low calcium.
For evisceration, cover with sterile saline-moistened dressings and call the surgeon.
Use the incentive spirometer and early walking to prevent lung problems after surgery.

compare.title: Wound dehiscence and evisceration
rows: Organs push out through the wound
Cover with sterile saline-moist dressing, notify

summary: This chapter covers clients whose bodies are failing to keep balance, such as those with fluid and electrolyte problems, shock, breathing or heart emergencies, and brain injuries. The exam asks you to spot changes early and act in the right order.

High potassium can cause tall, peaked T waves and dangerous rhythms, while low potassium causes muscle weakness and flat T waves. Too much fluid shows as crackles, swelling and weight gain; too little shows as a fast pulse, dry mouth and low urine output. In shock, an early sign is a rising heart rate and restlessness, and low blood pressure often comes later. In sepsis, draw blood cultures before starting antibiotics, and do not delay either.

For heart rhythms, ventricular fibrillation needs CPR and defibrillation, while asystole needs CPR and medicine but no shock. In normal sinus rhythm, a P wave comes before every evenly spaced QRS, while atrial fibrillation is irregular and raises stroke risk. Rising pressure in the skull often first shows as a change in level of consciousness. If a chest tube comes out of the chest, cover the site with a sterile dressing taped on three sides. Know how DKA and HHS differ.

concepts.definition: High potassium, often from kidney failure, can cause muscle weakness, tall peaked T waves and life-threatening rhythms. Low potassium, often from diuretics or vomiting, causes muscle weakness, cramps, flat T waves, U waves and rhythm problems.
concepts.tip: Peaked T waves = potassium too high. Low potassium also raises the risk of digoxin toxicity.

concepts.definition: Too much fluid causes crackles in the lungs, swelling, bounding pulse and weight gain. Too little causes a fast weak pulse, dry mouth, low urine output and dizziness on standing.
concepts.tip: Daily weight, at the same time with the same scale, is the best way to track fluid.

concepts.definition: Shock means organs are not getting enough blood. Early signs include a rising heart rate, restlessness and cool, pale skin. Blood pressure often falls later.
concepts.tip: Do not wait for low blood pressure; a rising pulse and new anxiety are early clues.

concepts.definition: Sepsis is a life-threatening body response to infection. Care includes blood cultures, then broad antibiotics without delay, IV fluids and close watching of blood pressure and urine output.
concepts.tip: Cultures first, then antibiotics, but do not hold antibiotics for long to get cultures.

concepts.definition: In normal sinus rhythm, a P wave comes before every evenly spaced QRS. In atrial fibrillation, there are no clear P waves, the baseline is wavy and the QRS complexes are unevenly spaced. Blood can pool in the heart and form clots, which raises stroke risk.
concepts.tip: Irregular rhythm with no clear P waves: think atrial fibrillation and ask about blood thinners.

concepts.definition: Ventricular fibrillation (chaotic waves, no QRS) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are treated with CPR and defibrillation. Asystole (a nearly flat line) and pulseless electrical activity are treated with CPR and epinephrine, not shocks.
concepts.tip: No electrical activity, nothing to shock: asystole gets CPR, not a shock.

source.org: American Heart Association (Guidelines for CPR and ECC)

concepts.definition: Rising pressure inside the skull. The earliest sign is often a change in level of consciousness. Later signs include a rising systolic blood pressure with a slow pulse and irregular breathing (Cushing's triad).
concepts.tip: Keep the head of the bed raised and the head in line with the body; avoid things that raise pressure, such as straining.

points: Match ECG changes to potassium: peaked T waves high, flat T and U waves low.
Daily weight is the best measure of fluid change.
A rising heart rate and restlessness are early shock signs; low blood pressure often comes later.
On a strip: normal sinus rhythm has a P wave before each even QRS; atrial fibrillation is irregular; shock ventricular fibrillation, not asystole.
A change in level of consciousness is often the first sign of rising pressure in the skull.
If a chest tube falls out, cover the site with a sterile dressing taped on three sides.
